objectives: State the chain rule + n-gram approximation.

slides.title: Probabilistic language models: chain rule + n-grams
slides.body:
A **language model** assigns probability to sequences. By the chain rule:
$$P(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n P(w_i \mid w_1, \dots, w_{i-1})$$

Each factor is the conditional probability of the next word given the history.

**The data problem**: history $w_1 \dots w_{i-1}$ grows linearly. Direct estimation is impossible (the exact full history is unique most of the time).

**N-gram approximation**: limit history to the last $n-1$ tokens.
$$P(w_i \mid w_1, \dots, w_{i-1}) \approx P(w_i \mid w_{i-n+1}, \dots, w_{i-1})$$

- **Unigram** ($n=1$): $P(w_i)$. Each word independent. Atomically primitive.
- **Bigram** ($n=2$): $P(w_i \mid w_{i-1})$. The classic.
- **Trigram** ($n=3$): $P(w_i \mid w_{i-2}, w_{i-1})$. Long the workhorse of speech recognition.
- **5-gram** ($n=5$): Google's web-scale LM (2006) was a 5-gram. Storage scaled to TB.

**Maximum-likelihood estimation**:
$$P_{MLE}(w_i \mid w_{i-1}) = \frac{c(w_{i-1}, w_i)}{c(w_{i-1})}$$
where $c$ is count in the training corpus.

**The sparsity problem**: most n-grams of moderate $n$ NEVER appear in training. So MLE gives them probability 0 — the model's probability for any unseen text is 0 (under the product). Must SMOOTH.

slides.title: Smoothing: Laplace, Good-Turing, Kneser-Ney
slides.body:
**Laplace smoothing (add-one)**:
$$P_{Laplace}(w_i \mid w_{i-1}) = \frac{c(w_{i-1}, w_i) + 1}{c(w_{i-1}) + V}$$
where $V$ = vocab size. Adds 1 fake count to every bigram. Smoothes but heavily overestimates rare events when $V$ is large.

**Good-Turing**: estimate the probability of unseen events from the frequency-of-frequencies. Adjusts the MLE counts so the total mass redistributes from seen → unseen.

**Kneser-Ney** (1995, the classic before neural LMs): adjusts based on **continuation count** — how many DIFFERENT contexts a word appears in. The intuition: a word like 'Francisco' has high unigram count but appears almost exclusively after 'San'; it should have LOW marginal probability in novel contexts. Standard MLE overestimates 'Francisco' standalone.
$$P_{KN}(w_i \mid w_{i-1}) = \frac{\max(c(w_{i-1}, w_i) - D, 0)}{c(w_{i-1})} + \lambda(w_{i-1}) P_{KN-cont}(w_i)$$
where $D$ is a discount, $\lambda$ a normalization, $P_{KN-cont}$ the continuation distribution.

Kneser-Ney was the SOTA for ~15 years. Modified Kneser-Ney + interpolated KN improvements pushed n-gram LM perplexity as low as it would go.

**Neural LMs supplanted KN around 2015**. Recurrent LMs (RNN-LM, LSTM) handled long-context naturally; transformer LMs (GPT, BERT) handled it even better. n-gram LMs survive in: KenLM library (used as a feature for ASR + MT decoding), federated mobile next-word prediction (resource-constrained), and as a teaching example.

slides.title: Perplexity + cross-entropy
slides.body:
**Cross-entropy** of model $Q$ relative to true distribution $P$:
$$H(P, Q) = -\mathbb{E}_{P}[\log Q]$$

In practice, estimated as the average negative log-likelihood on held-out data:
$$H = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_i \log Q(w_i \mid \text{context})$$

**Perplexity** = $2^H$ (binary log) or $e^H$ (natural log). Intuitive interpretation: 'on average, the model thinks the next word has 1 out of PPL equally-likely choices'.

- PPL = 1: perfect prediction.
- PPL = $V$: random (uniform over vocab).
- PPL = 50: model treats next word as if there were 50 plausible options. Strong LM territory.
- PPL = 10: very strong. Modern LLMs.

**Perplexity benchmarks**:
- 1990s n-gram on WSJ: ~200.
- 2010s LSTM on Penn Treebank: ~60.
- 2018 transformer-XL on enwik8: 0.99 bits-per-character (BPC), equivalent to PPL ~2 per char.
- GPT-3 on common LM benchmarks: PPL 10-20.

**Caveats**:
- Perplexity is tokenizer-dependent. PPL with 50K vocab and 100K vocab not directly comparable.
- Held-out data must come from a comparable distribution. Wikipedia-trained LM tested on legal text: very high PPL.
- PPL ≠ task performance. Sometimes a higher-PPL model better generates / understands / answers.

Still, perplexity remains THE standard intrinsic metric for autoregressive LMs.

question.question: Derive bigram MLE from a tiny corpus
question.goal: Corpus: 'the cat sat on the mat'. Compute $P(\text{sat} \mid \text{cat})$ + $P(\text{the} \mid \text{on})$.

steps.prompt: Count $c(\text{cat, sat})$ (occurrences of bigram 'cat sat'). Count $c(\text{cat})$ (occurrences of 'cat'). MLE: $P(\text{sat} \mid \text{cat}) = c(\text{cat, sat}) / c(\text{cat})$. What are these counts?

steps.reveal: $P(\text{sat} \mid \text{cat}) = 1/1 = 1$. With only 1 occurrence in tiny corpus, MLE is degenerate.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{P_{MLE}(w_i \mid w_{i-1}) = c(w_{i-1}, w_i) / c(w_{i-1})}$$ MLE is the bigram estimator. Tiny corpora give degenerate counts: most events are 0/1. On Wikipedia-scale corpora, MLE gives sensible relative frequencies for common bigrams + still requires smoothing for rare ones. The vast majority of possible bigrams in any natural language have count 0; smoothing redistributes mass to them.

question.question: A unigram model trained on 100B tokens has PPL 800 on a held-out set. A trigram model has PPL 120. A neural transformer LM has PPL 15. What does the rapid improvement tell us?
options: The neural LM is better designed.

Each step (unigram → trigram → neural) uses MORE context information. Unigram ignores context entirely (PPL near vocab size). Trigram uses 2 previous tokens. Neural uses many tokens + learns nonlinear patterns. Each unlocks a different part of language predictability.
question.explanation: Unigram only models marginal word frequency; perplexity scales with vocabulary size (~800 for 50K vocab is reasonable). Trigram adds bigram context (~120 captures common collocations). Neural LMs capture long-range dependencies, semantics, syntax. The PPL drops are real + reflect the model's ability to use more context. The transformer is using effectively unlimited context window (up to 32K-1M tokens in modern LLMs).

hints: How much context does each model use?
What predictability comes from each context size?
slides.workedSolution: Unigram: 0 context → PPL bounded below by entropy of word distribution (~6-8 nats for English ≈ PPL 400-1500). Trigram: 2 tokens → captures common phrases. Neural: full context → captures topic, syntax, semantics, world knowledge. Each level of context unlocks more predictability. Modern LLMs operate at PPL ~10 — close to the irreducible entropy of natural language.

question.question: Model assigns probability $P(\text{sequence}) = 0.001$. Sequence length 10 tokens. Per-token perplexity?
Choosing a decoder for a translation system
question.prompt: Your machine translation system gives high-perplexity outputs in greedy decoding. Walk through beam-search, sampling, + nucleus sampling — when each is right + the cost trade-offs.
Explain in two or three sentences why perplexity is the universal intrinsic metric for language models, despite its limitations.
question.rubric: Mentions that perplexity directly measures the model's average prediction confidence on held-out data, requires no task-specific labels, scales across architectures (n-gram, RNN, transformer), and has clear theoretical grounding in cross-entropy. The limitations (tokenizer-dependence, doesn't always predict downstream-task performance) don't undermine its core utility as a comparative metric for LMs trained with the same tokenizer.
